78: The trompo rules this taqueria, and its yield is calculated, not assumed. The kit's calculator starts from a 30 lb (13.6 kg) cone of raw meat with 8% adobo, and it assumes about 65% yield after cooking loss, drip and trimmings. At 1.5 oz (43 g) of cooked meat per taco, that is about 208 tacos per cone, or roughly 6.9 tacos per pound of raw meat. These are kit estimates: no source we found publishes the cooking loss of al pastor, so measure it yourself. Weigh the raw cone and the leftover at close, log it for a few weeks and carry the average into the Taco Cost & Trompo Yield Calculator. Measure in the calculator, recalculate in the plan. A street taco al pastor costs about $1.00 in ingredients with waste included, a food cost of 25% on its $4.00 menu price (kit estimate). Carnitas, suadero and barbacoa yield less, because of the confit and the long cook.
79: Equipment is bought with a price and a source, not by eye. The case budgets {{inv_trompo}} for two gas vertical broilers, one for the al pastor cone and a second cone or a spare. Catalog prices on WebstaurantStore run from $999 for a three-burner Avantco VB203 to $2,844 for a four-burner Visvardis model, so ask your dealer for a quote with installation and delivery. The griddle and comal come to {{inv_plancha}}. The fryer, the range for carnitas and guisados, the steam table and the tortilla warmers add up to {{inv_freidora}}. The Type I hood with UL 300 fire suppression and makeup air is {{inv_campana}} (published ranges run from $5,000 to $25,000, so get quotes for your own space), and the walk-in cooler is {{inv_camara}}. The refrigerated prep table, salsa bar and freezer come to {{inv_frio}}. A licensed gas contractor installs the gas line, and your city inspects it. A charcoal trompo is a different animal: it counts as solid-fuel cooking under NFPA 96, with its own exhaust, a spark arrestor and daily ash removal. It is a variant the Excel does not model, with more investment and a code that has to allow it. If the flavor tempts you, compare both budgets with real quotes, and ask the fire marshal in writing before you sign the lease.
80: Size production for your busiest Saturday, not for the average day. The case averages {{clientes_dia}} covers and {{ventas_dia}} in sales per opening day. Street tacos on a double 6 in (15 cm) tortilla mean the case goes through about 650 tortillas a day, counting quesadillas and gringas, and al pastor is the item that sets the cone schedule: you build, cook and slice cones through the day instead of one big batch at lunch. Two vertical broilers cover the peak with room to spare, so the trompo is rarely the limit; the hands slicing and the line behind them are. Ask for quotes with installation and lead time, because prices change by brand, and think about relief: a second taquero who can build and slice a cone means the whole shop does not hang on one person.
81: There is an alternative the financial plan does not model but the "Tortillas" tab of the calculator does: making your own tortillas with masa harina and a press, or going all the way to nixtamal, meaning corn cooked with slaked lime and ground into masa. The case buys its tortillas at opening, 6 in white corn tortillas that come 360 to a box, and it uses about 650 a day. Making your own with masa harina and a press starts to pay at around 660 a day, so at the case volume it is a product decision, not a saving. Nixtamal from the whole grain is a variant without an Excel: it needs a mill, a cooker and a tortilla machine, and a Tortilla Masters TM105 lists at $7,808, plus the labor to run it. A taqueria with its own tortilleria and a full bar is another business, closer to a full-service Mexican restaurant.
82: The case opens Tuesday through Sunday, with lunch from 11:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. and dinner from 5:00 to 10:00 p.m., and closes on Mondays and on the main holidays. Food safety rests on your written food safety plan. Hold the marinated al pastor cones at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, date-marked, and probe the meat at the start and in the middle of service, following the broiler rules your health department gives you in writing. Hold cut tomatoes, salsas and guacamole at 41 °F (5 °C) or below too, and run the salsa bar on rules: a clean container at every refill, a time stamp for put-out and discard, and one utensil per salsa. Dried chiles and achiote come from a specialty distributor and can take weeks to arrive, so keep a safety stock and a second supplier. Utilities average {{suministros_mes}} a month. Schedule the hood and duct cleaning to the NFPA 96 table and your fire marshal's requirements, and budget for maintenance.
85: The team in the case is short and designed so that nobody is irreplaceable. You are the head taquero and the GM: marinade, trompo, ordering (the chile distributor included) and management. The case pays you a modest wage, below what a manager would earn, and anything on top of that is an owner's draw from net profit; ask your CPA how your LLC is taxed. Beside you is a second taquero, a line cook on the trompo and griddle who can also marinate and slice, a prep cook for carnitas, guisados, aguas frescas and salsas, a counter lead who also works the register all year, part-time counter and expo staff for dinners and weekends, dish and prep help, and relief cover. That is {{plantilla_puestos}} people on the payroll, all W-2 employees.
86: With the relief coverage for vacations and days off, the schedule adds up to {{plantilla_puestos}} people, equal to {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents, and labor costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1 including employer payroll taxes of {{cargas_pct}}: {{personal_pct}} of sales. It is the biggest expense of the business, bigger than rent ({{ocupacion_anual}}, or {{ocupacion_pct}} of sales). The schedule covers {{cobertura_horas}} of the hours the shop needs: tight, with little room for sick days. The counter lead runs the register, the take-out orders, the marketplace tablet and the allergen questions, and the part-time staff cover the counter, the patio and pickup, with no drivers of your own. A Saturday night takes about five people and the annual schedule does not see it, so put it in the shift plan. Headcount grows by hiring people, not by a percentage, so add each new hire in the "Staffing" tab.
87: Pay every employee at least the highest of the federal minimum wage ($7.25 an hour, according to the Department of Labor, or {{salario_minimo_federal}} a year for a full-time employee at {{horas_semana}} hours a week), your state's and your city's, and remember that many states and cities are well above it. The case budgets at least $15 an hour and does not model a tip credit. Counter tips belong to the team through a tip jar or the POS screen; the owner and the managers do not take part in the pool. Hourly employees get overtime above 40 hours a week under the FLSA. Give every hire an offer letter in writing, complete Form I-9 and Form W-4 on day one, and keep accurate time records in the POS. Your accountant or payroll provider confirms which state and local rules apply to you.
88: One warning: never replace payroll staff with 1099 contractors who work your schedule under your direction. That is misclassification, and the IRS, the Department of Labor and your state can all come after you for back taxes and penalties. If you hire anyone under 18, federal and state rules limit their hours and ban some equipment, such as power-driven meat slicers, so check with the Department of Labor and your state before you schedule them. And think about the single-taquero risk: it is not a saving, it is a risk. If the only person who masters the trompo and the comal calls in sick, the taqueria closes, so a second taquero who can also marinate and slice is the best insurance you will ever pay for. Train that person from the start, not the day you need them, and split the marinade between the two of you so the recipe does not live in one head.
89: If you ever want your own drivers, they are W-2 employees, not independent contractors, and you need hired and non-owned auto liability on top of your general policy; check your state for the details. That is why the case sells through third-party delivery marketplaces instead, capped at {{plataforma_pct}} of sales with a commission of {{comision_pct}} on those orders, and with no drivers of its own. Do the math before you change that: a part-time driver's wages, payroll taxes, extra auto insurance and fuel or mileage against the marketplace commission on the same orders. Your own drivers only pay off with a high delivery volume or a short, dense delivery zone, and they carry the labor risk without the marketplace's storefront.
90: Train the team before you open. Every person who handles food needs a food handler card where your state or county requires one, and at least one person in charge needs the Certified Food Protection Manager (CFPM) certification under Food Code 2-102.12, if your jurisdiction has adopted it. Training should cover trompo and salsa temperatures, the 9 major allergens and cross-contact. Separately, you need trompo training: the marinade, building the cone, slicing and portioning. Then cover the OSHA basics: cuts from the trompo knife, burns from the griddle and the fryer, gas and heat are the typical accidents in this kitchen. Schedule a short refresher whenever someone new joins, because what is not repeated is forgotten.
93: To open, you need {{necesidad_caja}} in cash. Startup costs without working capital come to {{capex}}: build-out, hood, kitchen and launch, plus a security deposit of 2 months, {{meses_alquiler_previo}} months of rent paid before you open, and a contingency. Working capital adds {{fondo_maniobra}}. You fund it with {{fondos_propios}} of your own money ({{aportacion_pct}} of the cash needed) and a loan of {{prestamo}} at {{tipo_prestamo}} (nominal, not APR) over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, a typical SBA 7(a) structure with no interest-only period, with an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}}. Sales tax you pay on purchases is part of the cost (the workbook recovers none); exemptions such as resale certificates depend on your state, so confirm them with your accountant.
94: The three-year profit and loss projects revenue, excluding sales tax, of {{ventas_a1}}, {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}. Gross margin in year 1 is {{margen_bruto_pct}}, after all the variable costs: cost of goods ({{cogs_pct}} of sales), disposables, delivery marketplace fees, card processing and contingency. Labor adds up to {{personal_a1}}, rent to {{ocupacion_anual}} ({{ocupacion_pct}} of sales) and marketing to {{marketing_anual}}. EBITDA, earnings before depreciation, interest and taxes, is {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales. Net profit is {{resultado_neto_a1}}, {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}; the net margin in year 1 is {{margen_neto_a1}}, after an effective income tax rate of {{impuesto_beneficios}}. The example applies it as if the business paid corporate income tax (an LLC can elect it); as a pass-through, set the rate to 0 on "0. Assumptions" and budget your personal tax, and confirm how you are taxed with your CPA. To be honest about food cost: {{food_cost_comida}} on food is the average of the whole menu with its waste, not the al pastor taco alone, which sits near 25% on its menu price. The example prices pork shoulder at $3.00 a pound and bought corn tortillas at about $0.16 each, both kit estimates, so put in your supplier's prices. Every point of food cost on food sales takes about 1% of food sales straight out of profit, so after labor it is the number that moves the year the most.
95: Growth is the one the Excel applies: covers rise {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3, from {{clientes_dia}} to {{clientes_a2}} and {{clientes_a3}} a day, with the same average check of {{ticket}} excluding sales tax, and staff grows by hiring people, not by a percentage. Sales are about {{comida_pct}} food and {{bebida_pct}} beverages (aguas frescas, soft drinks and Mexican beer), with a cost of goods of {{food_cost_comida}} on food and {{food_cost_bebida}} on beverages. The workbook uses one example sales tax rate of {{sales_tax}} and keeps it out of revenue: you collect it from guests and remit it to the state. Rates, and whether take-out is taxed differently from dine-in, vary by state and city, so check with your state revenue department.
96: Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day, or {{equilibrio_ventas}} a year in revenue. Cash break-even (loan payments in, depreciation out) is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} covers a day, or {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}}, and leaves a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}} over the plan. The cash figure is the one to watch, because it is the one that pays the bank. The case has no interest-only period, so the margin is the same from year 1, but if you negotiate one it will look better until principal payments start: check the later years in the workbook before you celebrate. The {{clientes_dia}} covers a day on {{aforo}} indoor seats imply {{rotaciones_dia}} seat turns a day, but covers include guests who take the tacos home or have them delivered and never sit at a table.
97: The cash flow numbers the months from 1 to 12, and Month 1 is January, in calendar order. Sales start below full pace and build over the first months, which means the ramp falls on January and February, the softest months of the year, and that is why the working capital reserve matters. The lowest cash balance, {{saldo_minimo}}, comes in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}. With 12 pay periods there are no extra payments to plan for. Sales tax is remitted on your state's schedule; the workbook assumes you file quarterly, and if your state requires monthly filing, move the payments accordingly. Remember the tax is the guests' money, not yours, and keep it out of your working capital. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row of the Excel.
98: The lowest DSCR, or debt service coverage ratio, is {{dscr_min}}, and in year 1 it is {{dscr_a1}}: the business covers its debt with room to spare over the {{dscr_objetivo}} that lenders usually look for. That is a typical guideline, not a rule, and a bank will still want to see your sales plan. Payback, in years and before debt, is {{payback}} counting working capital, and {{payback_capex}} counting startup costs alone. This is not a fast-payback investment; it is a craft business that pays you a modest wage, with an owner's draw from net profit on top, and returns the capital with patience.
99: The pessimistic scenario is a weak year: {{pesimista_clientes}} covers a day at an average check of {{pesimista_ticket}} over {{pesimista_dias}} days gives sales of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}. In the optimistic one, {{optimista_clientes}} covers at {{optimista_ticket}} over {{optimista_dias}} days give sales of {{optimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}}. The distance between the two separates a good year from a bad one. And remember: the Excel rules, and if you change a green cell, this document stays behind.
102: Most owners open as an LLC, which you file with your state, and many add an operating agreement; talk to your CPA about LLC versus S corp taxation. Then get an EIN from the IRS and register for a sales tax permit with your state. In the US, requirements stack in layers: federal, state, county and city, and each one has its own forms. Apply for the city or county business license and, before you sign anything, run a zoning check on the exact address for restaurant use, the hood and the patio. Submit your plans for plan review with the health department (Food Code 8-201.11 asks for plans before construction or remodeling), then get your building permit and, at the end, the certificate of occupancy. The workbook uses an example sales tax of {{sales_tax}}, a single rate; some states tax to-go food differently, so check yours.
103: A gas trompo, a griddle and a fryer need a Type I hood with a fire suppression system (UL 300) and makeup air, plus a duct to the roof. The grease interceptor is part of the plumbing plan. If the building cannot take the duct, the concept does not fit, so settle it before you sign the lease. A charcoal trompo, like a charcoal grill, falls under NFPA 96 as solid-fuel cooking: a dedicated exhaust that serves only solid-fuel appliances, a spark arrestor, ashes removed at least once a day into a metal container and fuel stored away from the fire. That is a variant the case does not model. Your city decides, and local fire and mechanical codes differ, so ask the fire marshal in writing: hood? suppression? solid fuel allowed? Never assume the hood is optional. The case budgets the Type I hood, suppression and makeup air at {{inv_campana}}.
104: Before opening you need a health permit and a pre-opening inspection, after the plan review above. At least one person in charge should hold a Certified Food Protection Manager (CFPM) certificate (Food Code 2-102.12), and food handler cards depend on your state or county. The FDA Food Code 2022 is the model, but each state adopts its own edition. Hold cold food at 41 °F (5 °C) or below and hot food (carnitas, birria, guisados on the steam table) at 135 °F (57 °C) or above, and reheat to 165 °F (74 °C) within 2 hours. Cut tomatoes are TCS foods, so pico de gallo and fresh salsas are too; treat guacamole as TCS and ask your regulator. For the salsa bar, time as a public health control (TPHC, Food Code 3-501.19) allows 4 hours, or 6 if you start at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, but only with a written procedure and the hours marked.
105: Al pastor on the trompo is where your county has the final word. The cooking temperature and the maximum time the meat may stay on the broiler are set locally: county guides we reviewed ask for 145 °F (63 °C) in some places and 155 °F (68 °C) in others, with chicken at 165 °F (74 °C), and they ask you to slice only what has reached temperature and to use a fast-response probe. That is why this plan gives no single number as a rule. Get your health department's vertical broiler rules in writing (cook temp, max time on the broiler, leftover cone), write them into your trompo SOP and train the team on them. Reheat the leftover cone to 165 °F (74 °C) if the rules allow you to keep it at all.
106: Tell guests about allergens: the US recognizes 9 major allergens, including sesame (FASTER Act, effective January 1, 2023). In a taqueria, salsa macha is the one to watch, because this chile oil is made with peanuts and sesame, and moles can carry tree nuts, peanuts and sesame. Flour tortillas for the gringas are wheat, cheese and crema are milk and beer is wheat and barley. Label every salsa at the salsa bar and keep an allergen sign next to it. Do not promise "gluten-free": under 21 CFR 101.91 the claim means less than 20 ppm of gluten, and a comal or fryer shared with flour tortillas makes it impossible to guarantee. The honest line is "corn tortillas are naturally gluten-free; ask about our fryer and griddle". Check your state and city for other required public notices as well, such as consumer advisories and posting rules.
107: If you serve beer and wine, you need a license from your state's alcohol beverage control (ABC) agency plus local approval. Cost and timing vary enormously from state to state and from city to city, so apply early, write a contingency into your lease and never open counting on a license you do not have yet. A beer and wine license does not cover liquor, and the case has none. Your insurance, budgeted at {{seguros_anual}} a year in the case, should combine general liability with liquor liability, property and workers' compensation. Staff are W-2 employees paid by the hour, never 1099 contractors, and your state or city minimum wage applies. Playing recorded music in the shop needs licenses from ASCAP, BMI and SESAC, and some cities have packaging ordinances for take-out containers, so ask the city before you order boxes.
108: Selling tacos from your home kitchen is another matter. There is no federal rule, and state cottage food laws cover low-risk products; marinated meat and fresh salsas are TCS foods, so this plan assumes a permitted shop, and you should check your state before you try anything else. This section lists what we can state with confidence; for everything else, check with your accountant, your city or the health inspector before you decide. A note for UK readers: register your food business with your local council at least 28 days before you open, expect a Food Hygiene Rating of 0 to 5 (FHIS in Scotland), VAT at 20% on hot food and on food eaten in (hot tacos to take away included), 14 allergens to declare (peanuts and sesame in the macha, celery and mustard depending on the recipe, and sulphites), and a premises plus a personal licence if you sell alcohol.
111: The conclusion is that a taco shop of this size is viable, but demanding. With {{clientes_dia}} covers a day at an average check of {{ticket}} excluding sales tax, year 1 leaves a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}} and a cash margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}}. The lowest DSCR is {{dscr_min}}, the lowest cash balance is {{saldo_minimo}} in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, which is January, and the payback, in years and before debt, is {{payback}}. Check the later years in the workbook before you commit. This is not a business to open with tight capital.
112: The first risk, and the most expensive, is signing a lease for a space where the exhaust cannot reach the roof. Without it there is no trompo, griddle or fryer: ask the city and a mechanical contractor before you sign. The second is running the trompo without a protocol: a cone with no build time or time limit, marinated meat held above 41 °F (5 °C), or layers sliced before they are done. Get your county's vertical broiler rules in writing, write the protocol and check the temperature with a probe. The third is not measuring the yield of the trompo: cooking loss and leftover cone quietly eat your margin. Weigh the raw cone and the leftover every day, measure in the calculator and recalculate in the plan with your real data.
113: The fourth is a salsa bar without rules: with no clean container at each refill, no time stamp for put-out and discard and no utensil per salsa, it is the place where things go wrong fastest. The fifth is promising "gluten-free" with the comal and the fryer shared with flour tortillas: you do not promise it. The sixth is treating the beer and wine license as an afterthought, when it can take months and varies by state and city. Apply as soon as you sign the lease and never open counting on it. Review with your accountant how your state taxes take-out and dine-in before you set up the POS, because a tax error repeats on every ticket, hundreds of times a year.
114: The seventh is depending on a single chile distributor: it can take weeks to deliver, so keep a safety stock and a second supplier. The eighth is making your own tortillas to save money: below roughly 660 tortillas a day it does not pay. The ninth is opening your doors to the marketplaces without doing the math: between the commission, the promotions and the packaging, the register eats the margin, which is why the case caps them at {{plataforma_pct}} of sales. And one risk decides the plan: the cash of years 2 and 3. With a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}} in the case, there is not much room. Track covers every month against the {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} covers a day you need at cash break-even, and keep in mind that the pessimistic scenario closes with a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}.
115: The tenth is the single taquero: one sick day closes the shop, so train a second person early who can marinate, build the cone and slice. The eleventh is selling the taqueria as Tex-Mex: it is not, and with that sign you attract people looking for burritos and nachos when you sell street tacos, tortilla chips and real salsas. None of these is expensive to avoid if you see it in time, and all of them are expensive if you find out after opening. Review these points with your accountant and your team before you open, and go back to them after three months, when the daily work piles up and the important things get pushed back.
116: The action plan has six phases and 80 tasks in the checklist that comes with the kit. "Phase 1 - Business Setup" has 12 tasks. "Phase 2 - Hood, Gas & Permits" has 15. "Phase 3 - Kitchen & Health" has 14. "Phase 4 - Staff & Allergens" has 13. "Phase 5 - Menu, Brand, Delivery" has 13. And "Phase 6 - Opening & 90 Days" has 13. Follow the order: the zoning check and the fire marshal's answer on the hood and the duct come before you sign the lease, the beer and wine license application goes in as soon as you do, and your county's vertical broiler rules in writing come before you buy the trompo. Check off each task when you close it, and if one slips, see what depends on it before you move the opening date.
117: The next step is to fill in the Excel with your own numbers: your real rent, your average check, your covers, your loan, your staff and your opening calendar. Change only the green cells; this document reflects the example case, and yours is set by your spreadsheet. Then measure your trompo and cost your whole menu with the Taco Cost & Trompo Yield Calculator, not just the al pastor taco. With your own data in front of you, come back to this section and check what is left in cash in years 2 and 3 if the year turns out like the pessimistic scenario. If the cash holds up, you have a solid plan to take to the bank; if not, adjust the investment, the staffing or the calendar before you sign anything.
